title: The colors of the spirit
hookLine: Emerson: nature always wears the colors of the spirit
carry: the world wears the colors of my spirit
last: AMONG TREES, REASON AND FAITH COME BACK TOGETHER.

lines: GLAD TO THE BRINK OF FEAR.
WHERE DID THE GLADNESS COME FROM?
cards: Snow puddles. Twilight. A cloudy sky.

A bare, open stretch of town land with nothing on it. Emerson is crossing it, with no special good fortune on his mind, he says so himself. And yet: "I have enjoyed a perfect exhilaration. I am glad to the brink of fear."

On the dullest ground in town, at the dullest hour, he's almost frightened by how happy he is. You crossed that ground with him on day one thousand twenty-two. Today's question: where did the gladness come from?

teach.h: THE DELIGHT ISN'T ONLY IN NATURE.
teach.b: First, where the delight lives. Later in the same chapter, Emerson says it plainly: the power to produce this delight does not reside in nature, but in man, or in a harmony of both.
The landscape doesn't hand out joy on its own; something in the one looking has to meet it. Second, the line.
"Nature always wears the colors of the spirit." The same field can look like a gift or a wasteland, depending on who's crossing it. Third, he doesn't only mean happy colors.
"To a man laboring under calamity, the heat of his own fire hath sadness in it."

teach.h: EVEN THE FIRE HAS SADNESS IN IT.
teach.b: The fire is the same fire, and warm, but to someone in trouble even warmth looks sad. He goes further: someone who has just lost a dear friend to death, he says, feels a kind of contempt for the landscape.
The sky itself seems less grand. These are not the words of a man who's never grieved. Fourth, what to do with this.
It's not a scolding, and not a trick of positive thinking. It's a description.

If the street looks gray today, part of the gray may be yours. That isn't a failure; it's information. And it works the other way: some afternoon the laundromat might look almost holy, and that may be yours too.
Knowing the view wears your colors lets you hold your moods a little more lightly.

how: Readers of Emerson sometimes use this passage from Nature to notice how mood shapes what they see, checking their own state before deciding a place or a day is dreary.

games.q: what does “the colors of the spirit” mean?
o: the bright colors of autumn leaves in New England
Emerson's idea that our moods tint how the world looks
a painter's palette for showing holy figures

games.q: inside the colors of the spirit: tap the pairs.
p: in man, or a harmony of both

s: Emerson says the beauty lives only in the landscape
he says the power to delight is in us, or in a harmony of both.
his happiest moment in the passage comes on a dreary evening
snow puddles, twilight, a cloudy sky, and he is glad to the brink of fear.
Emerson writes only about nature's happy colors
he writes that to someone under calamity, even the warmth of his own fire has sadness in it.

games.q: you're crossing a bare, muddy patch of ground at twilight, with no special good fortune on your mind. what does Emerson say he felt there?
o: bored, and in a hurry to get home.
a perfect exhilaration, glad to the brink of fear.
games.why: on the dullest ground at the dullest hour, he was almost frightened by how glad he was. the gladness came from the one crossing.

practice: Look at whatever is in front of you, a wall, a window, a street, and first just see it. Then ask what your mood is right now, tired, easy, tense, hopeful, and look again, noticing the color that mood is lending the room.
Don't try to change it; let the breath settle and look one more time.

wordCard.voice: The colors of the spirit. Emerson's claim that nature always wears them: the same field, the same fire, looks glad or grieving depending on the one who sees. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the world wears the colors of my spirit. The field hasn't changed; you have, for now. Until tomorrow.
